newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: U.S. survivor of KAL jet crash dies in hospital.
newsitem.headline: U.S. survivor of KAL jet crash dies in hospital.

text.p: An American woman, one of 29 people who survived last week's Korean Air Lines jet crash, has died in hospital after suffering severe burns, an airline spokesman said on Monday.

Grace Chung, a U.S. citizen whose family immigrated from Taiwan, was one of four people being treated in a U.S. military burns centre in Texas for injuries suffered in the crash on the Pacific island of Guam.
"All the four passengers suffered serious burns and were sent to a military hospital in San Antonio," the spokesman said. The other three are South Koreans.
Korean Air Lines (KAL) Flight 801, with 254 people on board, slammed into hillside jungle three miles (five km) from Guam's International airport on Wednesday.
Among the 28 survivors were three Americans, one Japanese and one New Zealander. The rest were South Koreans, KAL said.
Officials of the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), said on Sunday 140 bodies had been recovered and were awaiting identification. Most of the other remains were badly mangled.

"We are prepared to repatriate the remains of South Koreans killed in the crash. Some relatives want immediate repatriation while others want to wait until all the remains are identified," the KAL spokesman said.

NTSB officials said preliminary examination of the engines, the wreckage and data from the flight recorders showed that the plane was in full control on a steady descent and that the crew were not aware of any impending disaster.

The NTSB, which is also looking into the possibility that an unusually heavy downpour and sudden loss of visibility could have contributed to the crash, has not determined whether human error was the cause.
The Seoul government said on Monday it planned to set up a $118 million medical centre to cope with disasters requiring urgent medical attention.

"The medical centre could provide quick medical support to people requiring emergency treatment after plane crashes, building collapses, landslides or other calamities," said Yoo Keun-hyock, a health and welfare ministry official.
He said the ministry, in cooperation with other government agencies, planned to present a bill to set up the centre to parliament this year.
